L4: # Orthographic
L5: ## Description
L6: 
L7: The orthographic projection is an azimuthal perspective projection, projecting the Earth's surface from an infinite distance to a plane. It gives the illusion of a three-dimensional globe so it is often used as an inset map or for pictorial views of the Earth from space. This map projection is the same as the cite1†local projection but only supports spheres.
L8: It is believed that the projection was developed by the Egyptians and the Greeks. It is available in ArcGIS Pro 1.0 and later and in ArcGIS Desktop 8.1.1 and later.
L9: 
L10: cite2†Image: An example of the orthographic projection L11: 
L12: The orthographic map projection is shown centered on the Caribbean.
L13: ## Projection properties
L14: 
L15: The subsections below describe the orthographic projection properties.
L16: ### Graticule
L17: 
L18: Orthographic is an azimuthal projection available in three aspects.
L19: 
L20: In the polar aspect, the meridians project as straight lines originating at the pole in the center. Angles between them are true. The parallels are shown as unequally spaced concentric circular arcs. Their spacing decreases with the distance from the center. All graticule line intersections are 90 degrees. The opposite pole cannot be projected. The graticule is symmetric across any meridian.
L21: In the equatorial aspect, the equator and the central meridian are projected as two perpendicular straight lines. Two meridians, 90 degrees east and west of the central meridian, project as a circle and represent the edge of the projection. The other meridians are complex curves. Their spacing decreases away from the central meridian. All parallels are straight lines, perpendicular to the central meridian. Their spacing decreases away from the equator. Both poles project as points at the projection's edge.
L22: The graticule is symmetric across the equator and the central meridian.
L23: In the oblique case, only the central meridian and antimeridian project as straight lines. The other meridians are semiellipses intersecting at the pole nearest to the center, which is projected as a point. The parallels are unequally spaced complete or partial ellipses and their spacing decreases away from the projection's center. The graticule is symmetric across the central meridian.
L24: ### Distortion
L25: 
L26: The orthographic projection is neither conformal nor equal-area. Shapes, areas, distances, directions, and angles are all generally distorted. Only the center of the map is free of distortion. Distortion values greatly increase radially from the origin.
L27: 
L28: ## Usage
L29: 
L30: The oblique aspect of this projection can be used as an inset locator map or for pictorial views of the Earth from space.
L31: ## Variants
L32: 
L33: There are two variants available in ArcGIS:
L34: 
L35:   * The orthographic variant uses the semimajor axis for the radius and equations for a sphere. It does not support the ellipsoid. It is available in ArcGIS Pro 1.0 and later and in ArcGIS Desktop 8.1.1 and later.
L36:   * The orthographic auxiliary sphere variant uses sphere-based equations with a sphere specified by the Auxiliary Sphere Type parameter. It does not support the ellipsoid. It is available in ArcGIS Pro 1.0 and later and in ArcGIS Desktop 9.3 and later.
L37: ## Limitations
L38: 
L39: The orthographic projection is limited to one hemisphere and cannot display the whole world. Neither variant supports an ellipsoid.
L40: ## Parameters
L41: 
L42: Orthographic parameters are as follows:
L43: 
L44:   * False Easting
L45: 
L46:   * False Northing
L47: 
L48:   * Longitude Of Center
L49: 
L50:   * Latitude Of Center
L51: 
L52: Orthographic auxiliary sphere parameters are as follows:
L53: 
L54:   * False Easting
L55: 
L56:   * False Northing
L57: 
L58:   * Longitude Of Center
L59: 
L60:   * Latitude Of Center
L61: 
L62:   * Auxiliary Sphere Type, with values as follows:
L63: 
L64:     * 0 = Use semimajor axis of the geographic coordinate system
L65: 
L66:     * 1 = Use semiminor axis
L67: 
L68:     * 2 = Calculate and use authalic radius
L69:     * 3 = Use authalic radius and convert geodetic latitudes to authalic latitudes
L70: ##### Note:
L71: 
L72: If the geographic coordinate system uses a sphere, the Auxiliary Sphere Type uses the radius of the sphere in all four cases.
L73: ## Sources
L74: 
L75: Snyder, J. P. (1987). Map Projections: A Working Manual. U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 1395. Washington, DC: United States Government Printing Office.
L76: 
L77: Snyder, J. P. (1993). Flattening the Earth. Two Thousand Years of Map Projections. Chicago and London: University of Chicago Press.
L78: 
L79: Snyder, J. P. and Voxland, P. M. (1989). An Album of Map Projections. U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 1453. Washington, DC: United States Government Printing Office.

L4: # Lambert azimuthal equal-area
L5: ## Description
L6: 
L7: The Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection maintains land features at their true relative sizes while simultaneously maintaining a true sense of direction from the center. The world is projected onto a flat surface from any point on the globe. Although all aspects are possible (equatorial, polar, and oblique), the one used most commonly is the polar aspect. This projection is best suited for individual land masses that are symmetrically proportioned, either round or square.
L8: The Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection was developed by Johann H. Lambert in 1772. It is available in ArcGIS Pro 1.0 and later and in ArcGIS Desktop 8.0 and later.
L9: 
L10: cite1†Image: An example of the Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection L11: 
L12: The Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centered on the south pole is shown.
L13: ## Projection properties
L14: 
L15: The subsections below describe the Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection properties.
L16: ### Graticule
L17: 
L18: Lambert azimuthal equal-area is an azimuthal projection with three aspects: polar, equatorial, and oblique.
L19: In the polar aspect, the meridians project as straight lines originating at the pole and the angles between them are true. The parallels are shown as unequally spaced concentric circular arcs and their spacing decreases with the distance from the center. All graticule line intersections are 90 degrees. The opposite pole is projected as a circle and presents the edge of the map. The graticule is symmetric across any meridian.
L20: In the equatorial aspect, the equator and the central meridian are projected as two perpendicular straight lines. Two meridians, 90 degrees east and west of the central meridian, project as a circle. Other meridians are complex curves. Their spacing decreases away from the central meridian. All parallels are complex curves concave toward the nearest pole and unequally spaced along the central meridian. The spacing of the parallels decreases away from the equator. Both poles project as points.
L21: The antipodal point of the projection's center projects as a circle and presents the edge of the map. The graticule is symmetric across the equator and the central meridian.
L22: In the oblique case, only the central meridian and antimeridian project as straight lines. The other meridians and parallels are complex curves. The meridians intersect at poles and are projected as a point. The parallels are unequally spaced along the central meridian and their spacing decreases away from the projection's center. The graticule is symmetric across the central meridian.
L23: ### Distortion
L24: 
L25: Lambert azimuthal equal-area is an equal-area (equivalent) projection. Shapes, directions, angles, and distances are generally distorted. Scale and directions are true only at the center of the projection. The scale decreases with the distance from the center along the radii and increases from the center perpendicularly to the radii, resulting in small shapes compressed radially from the center and elongated perpendicularly. The general pattern of distortion is radial.
L26: ## Usage
L27: 
L28: Although the Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection can display the entire globe, its practical usage is typically limited to a hemisphere. This projection is most commonly used for thematic mapping of polar regions. The oblique aspect is sometimes used for individual land masses that are symmetrically proportioned, either round or square.
L29: ## Variants
L30: 
L31: There are two variants available in ArcGIS.
L32: 
L33:   * Lambert azimuthal equal-area is available in ArcGIS Pro 1.0 and later and in ArcGIS Desktop 8.0 and later.
L34:   * Lambert azimuthal equal-area auxiliary sphere is available in ArcGIS Pro 1.0 and later and in ArcGIS Desktop 9.3 and later. This variant does not support the ellipsoid and uses sphere-based equations with a sphere specified by the Auxiliary Sphere Type parameter. Although resulting coordinates will not match the true ellipsoidal solution, the Lambert azimuthal equal-area auxiliary sphere variant maintains the equal-area property when the Auxiliary Sphere Type 3 is used.
L35: Otherwise, areas are not maintained for ellipsoids using this variant.
L36: ## Limitations
L37: 
L38: Only the Lambert azimuthal equal-area variant supports ellipsoids.
L39: ## Parameters
L40: 
L41: Lambert azimuthal equal-area parameters are as follows:
L42: 
L43:   * False Easting
L44: 
L45:   * False Northing
L46: 
L47:   * Central Meridian
L48: 
L49:   * Latitude Of Origin
L50: 
L51: Lambert azimuthal equal-area auxiliary sphere parameters are as follows:
L52: 
L53:   * False Easting
L54: 
L55:   * False Northing
L56: 
L57:   * Central Meridian
L58: 
L59:   * Latitude Of Origin
L60: 
L61:   * Auxiliary Sphere Type, with values as follows:
L62: 
L63:     * 0 = Use semimajor axis of the geographic coordinate system
L64: 
L65:     * 1 = Use semiminor axis
L66: 
L67:     * 2 = Calculate and use authalic radius
L68:     * 3 = Use authalic radius and convert geodetic latitudes to authalic latitudes
L69: ##### Note:
L70: 
L71: If the geographic coordinate system uses a sphere, the Auxiliary Sphere Type uses the radius of the sphere in all four cases.
